source_text: Manichaeus dicit, voluntatem malam ab ea inspirari natura, quae bonum velle non potest; voluntatem vero bonam ab ea infundi natura, quae malum velle non potest; ita utique naturis singularum rerum imponit necessitatem, ut propriae voluntates non possint velle contraria. Inter nos et illum certe grande chaos est; videamus nunc quantum ab eo tu recesseris. Dicis esse liberam voluntatem, sed ut malum tantummodo faciat, non autem esse in hoc liberam, ut malum desistat operari, nisi ei fuerit imposita necessitas volendi bonum, ab ea natura, quae, ut tuis utar sermonibus: malum non potest velle [n252] . Definis ergo genus hominum per liberum arbitrium nihil aliud quam peccare, nec aliud posse facere. Per quod absolute pronuntias, humanam naturam unum semper cupere quod malum est, et velle non posse contrarium; naturam autem Dei malum non posse velle; et ideo, nisi necessitatis suae participem fecerit malam hominum naturam, bonum in ea actionis esse non posse. Post haec itaque utrum non multum ames Manichaeum, in cordis tui secreto Deus viderit; quantum tamen ex dogmatum germanitate monstratur, nihil aliud prorsus egisti, quam ut ordine commutato idem quod ille affirmarat adstrueres.
pass_a_gloss: The Manichaean says that an evil will is inspired by that nature which cannot will good; but a good will is poured in by that nature which cannot will evil; so at any rate he imposes a necessity on the natures of the singular things, that their own wills cannot will contraries. Between us and him certainly there is a great chaos; let us see now how much you have receded from him. You say there is a free will, but that it may only do evil, but that it is not free in this, that it desist from working evil, unless a necessity of willing good shall have been imposed on it, from that nature which, that I may use your speeches: cannot will evil. You define therefore the kind of humans through free choice nothing other than to sin, nor to be able to do another thing. Through which you pronounce absolutely, that human nature always desires one thing which is evil, and cannot will the contrary; but the nature of God cannot will evil; and therefore, unless it shall have made the evil nature of humans a participant of its own necessity, there cannot be a good of action in it. After these things therefore whether you do not love the Manichaean much, God will have seen in the secret of your heart; how much nevertheless from the kinship of dogmas is shown, you have driven nothing other at all, than that with the order changed you would build up the same which he had affirmed.

pass_b_english: The Manichaean says that an evil will is inspired by a nature that cannot will good, while a good will is poured in by a nature that cannot will evil. Thus he imposes on the natures of each kind of thing a necessity such that their own wills cannot will the opposite. There is certainly a great gulf between him and us. Let us now see how far you have departed from him. You say that the will is free, but only to do evil; it is not free to cease doing evil unless a necessity of willing good is imposed on it by that nature which, to use your words, “cannot will evil” (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.7). You therefore define the human race as doing nothing through free choice except sinning, and as unable to do anything else. By this you declare outright that human nature always desires only one thing, evil, and cannot will the opposite. God's nature, however, cannot will evil; therefore, unless it makes evil human nature share in its own necessity, no good action can exist in human nature. After this, God may see in the secrecy of your heart whether you have little love for Mani. But as far as the kinship of your doctrines shows, you have done absolutely nothing except change the order and establish the same thing he asserted.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
